title: Interpolated Shape Batching: Padding Budgets & KV Warmup Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This playbook describes an operational approach for reducing padding-induced token waste and improving cold-start behavior of KV caches via an interpolated-shape batching strategy with explicit padding budgets and a lightweight KV warmup heuristic. Intended for serving-runtime implementers and SREs responsible for throughput/latency tradeoffs.

Context and motivation:
- Padding overhead is a dominant cost driver for routes with high variance in sequence length. Existing bucketing/packing reduces waste but either increases latency for short tails or fragments kernels when shapes are multimodal.
- KV cache cold starts (when requests hit new prefixes or after eviction) create latency spikes; naive warming increases cost. We need a principled, low-risk approach to: (1) reduce token-level padding waste, (2) keep tail latency bounded, (3) avoid excessive precomputation for KV warming.

Goals and success metrics:
- Reduce median token padding per-request by >= 30% for target user routes (measured by per-request padded_tokens / requested_tokens).
- Keep p95 latency regression <= 5% and p99 regression <= 10% compared to baseline packing.
- Reduce fraction of cold-KV hits producing > 1.5x latency spike by 50% during pilot.
- No customer-facing errors; safe rollback paths.

Design overview:
1) Shape interpolation concept:
- Instead of strict fixed-width buckets, we maintain a small set (N=6–12) of canonical "anchor" shapes per model (lengths like 8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512).
- Incoming request length L is mapped to an interpolated execution target by selecting either the nearest anchor or a linear-interpolated kernel mode between two anchors when workload indicates frequent intermediate lengths.
- Interpolation triggers the runtime to: a) apply soft-padding (pad to nearest anchor but allow small additional micro-rows with controlled budget); b) prefer kernels that support variable local padding (e.g., grouped attention kernels).

2) Per-route padding budgets:
- Each route has a configurable "padding budget" B (tokens per 1k requests). The budget is enforced probabilistically: when budget is exhausted, requests fallback to a stricter packing policy (bigger buckets) or to an expedited path (lower latency, higher cost).
- Budgets are enforced with a leaky-bucket counter per shard and aggregated to per-tenant view.
- Default budgets are suggested by Redwood Optimize profiles (derived from historical length distribution and cost targets).

3) Adaptive interpolation policy:
- Runtime maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) distribution of lengths per route + per-model. When intermediate lengths exceed a configured frequency threshold (e.g., 6% of traffic), the runtime enables interpolation between the two nearest anchors and creates a temporary micro-bucket for 60s.
- Micro-buckets are collapsed when traffic decreases below threshold or when kernel affinity indicates suboptimal utilization.

4) KV warmup heuristic (lightweight):
- When a request is routed to an anchor/micro-bucket with an uncached prefix (or eviction detected), the scheduler has two warmup options depending on latency headroom:
  a) Opportunistic warmup: piggyback KV prefetch on trailing requests that touch same session prefix (cheap, best-effort).
  b) Speculative warmup: when a request is predicted to cause > 50ms extra latency (past-profile), spawn a low-priority warmup job to populate KV for next 1–2 tokens. Cost-limited by budget per shard.
- Warmup decisions are scored by a simple utility function: U = alpha * predicted_latency_gain - beta * estimated_cost. Thresholds are tunable per deployment tier.

Scheduling & kernel selection integration:
- Kernel selector receives (anchor_id, micro_bucket_flag, estimated_sequence_length, padding_budget_available). It ranks kernels by a combined score: throughput_score * w_t + latency_score * w_l + cost_score * w_c + kernel_affinity_bonus.
- Interpolated mode exposes kernel flags (supports_variable_padding = true/false, kv_warmup_friendly = true/false) used to prefer kernels that avoid quadratic overhead from extra padding.
- When micro-buckets are active, continuous-batcher will attempt to coalesce micro-rows only within a small time window (T_micro = 8–12ms) to avoid increasing request wait.

Implementation details (pseudo-flow):
- On request arrival: determine length L, lookup EMA -> choose anchors a_lo, a_hi. If interpolation condition met and padding_budget > 0: enable interpolated path. Else select nearest anchor.
- Assign to in-flight micro-bucket if exists, else create micro-bucket (evict oldest micro-bucket if > M active).
- Kernel selection: call kernel_selector(anchor, micro_flag, kv_hint). Kernel returns chosen kernel id and predicted batch_size target.
- Submit to batcher with deadline = min(route_slo_deadline, T_micro + now).
- On dispatch: if kv_miss predicted, trigger opportunistic/speculative warmup subject to warmup budget.

Operational knobs and defaults:
- N anchors per model: default 8 (8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 192, 256, 512). Tunable.
- Micro-bucket TTL: default 60s.
- T_micro batching window: default 10ms.
- Padding budget B default: 200 tokens / 1k requests (per-route) for free-tier, higher for enterprise.
- Warmup alpha/beta default: alpha=1.2, beta=0.8 (units normalized).

Metrics to collect (per route/model/shard):
- padded_tokens_per_request, padded_token_ratio, per-bucket utilization, kernel_utilization, p50/p95/p99 latency, fraction_of_kv_miss_warmups, warmup_cost_tokens, budget_consumption_pct

Experiment plan & safety:
- Phase A (canary): enable read-only interpolation with metrics-only and simulated cost accounting; compare padded_token_ratio and p95 latency to baseline for 48h per route.
- Phase B (limited roll): enable for 5% of traffic on low-SLO routes; enforce strict budget, auto-fallback on p99 regressions. Monitor KV spike events.
- Phase C (broader roll): increase to 25% then 60% traffic with dynamic budget tuning from Redwood Optimize.
- Rollback: switch to nearest-anchor-only packing and flush micro-buckets. KV warmup tasks are stopped; existing warmup state may be retained for 5m.

Tradeoffs and failure modes:
- Interpolated micro-buckets can increase kernel fragmentation and reduce overall GPU throughput if traffic is too spiky. Mitigation: limit active micro-buckets per shard and prefer kernels with grouped-attention support.
- Speculative warmups may waste GPU cycles; budget enforcement and utility-scored decisions limit cost.
- Incorrect EMA hyperparameters may lead to oscillation; add hysteresis and cooldown for micro-bucket creation.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Optimal anchor set per-model: automate via offline clustering of token length histograms (follow-up PR to GH-rl-runtime).
- Better warmup signal: use token-level attention-sensitivity to prioritize which prefixes to warm.
- Integration with prefetch-aware GPUs (NVIDIA MPI) for cross-request KV prefetching.
- SRE-run playbook for handling warmup storms.

References and related artifacts:
- CON-1423: padding-budget telemetry dashboard (internal)
- GH-rl-runtime/PR-881: initial kernel-affinity API prototype
- slack:#runtime-kernels thread "kv-warmup-heuristics" for discussions

Appendix: quick heuristics checklist for on-call
- If p99 latency increases and padded_token_ratio went down: check micro-bucket count and kernel_utilization; consider increasing T_micro or collapsing micro-buckets.
- If warmup cost > budget: lower warmup alpha or raise warmup utility threshold.
- If sudden spike in KV misses: temporarily disable speculative warmup and enable opportunistic-only mode.

Author notes: this is intentionally conservative; initial rollout should be metrics-first. The next step is a small prototype in the dev cluster focusing on one low-SLO route (internal search) and feeding results into Redwood Optimize to auto-propose budgets.
